title: Click-Based Off-Policy Evaluation for Ranking
one_liner: To evaluate a new ranking system using old logged data, use user clicks instead of the logging system's choices, even if the old system was completely deterministic.
lead: When you change a ranking algorithm in production, you want to estimate how much better it performs before you deploy it, because bad changes cost real users and money. The problem: you only have offline data from the old system. If that old system always showed the same ranking regardless of what it saw, all the old methods for estimation fail catastrophically. This paper uses a hidden signal in the data — user click patterns — to fix the problem.

problem.h2: Why old methods break under deterministic logging
paras: A ranking system is a machine that takes a context (what you know: a user's interests, time of day, device) and outputs an ordered list. You want to evaluate a new ranking algorithm by replaying it on old logged data. The old data contains triples: the context, which ranked items the old system showed, and whether the user clicked on each item.

The standard trick for this problem is called inverse propensity scoring: when the new algorithm would have shown an item that the old system showed and the user clicked, count that click. When the new algorithm would have shown something the old system never ranked (because the old system was a fixed rule), assign it zero. The assumption: the old system was random enough that it showed diverse items. But when the old system is completely deterministic — it always ranks the same items in the same order regardless of context — it showed nothing but one fixed sequence. The old method sees only zeros and collapses.

A beginner tries: ignore the deterministic logging, try to train a new model directly on clicks from the old deterministic ranking. But this learns the old system's bias, not a better ranking, because the old system only ever ranked certain items, so the training data is skewed toward those items and the model copies that lopsidedness.

callout.html: Use the clicks themselves as a signal of importance, not the old system's choice.

object.h2: The single thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of using the logging policy's action probability (how likely the old system was to show that item), the method uses the user's click probability (how likely the user was to click on that item given they saw it). This shift means the importance weights now rest on user behavior, not system behavior.

hidden.h2: Click probability: what users actually respond to
hidden.name: User click probability
paras: Click probability is the fraction of times a user clicked on an item when they saw it. It is not the same as whether the old ranking system showed that item. Even if the old system never ranked Item 5, we can infer the user's click probability for Item 5 from other items' clicks and user context. If users clicked on Items 1 and 2 often but Item 3 rarely, we can estimate that Item 3 has low click appeal.

The paper estimates click probability by training a neural network on the logged data: given context and item, predict whether the user will click. This number becomes the new importance weight. Click probability exists and is independent even when the logging policy is fully deterministic, because what users click on does not depend on what the old system chose to show — it depends on what users actually prefer.

heat.caption: Darker means more informative for click prediction. Highlights: actual clicks and inferred user intent drive the reweighting.

reads.html: Click probability is how often a user clicks when they see an item. Even if a system is deterministic and never explores, users still click more on some items and less on others. That pattern is the hidden signal.
The paper averages over click events to estimate the new policy's value: sum over all items of (true click) times (click probability under new policy divided by click probability under old policy).

mechanism.h2: Why reweighting by clicks fixes deterministic logging
paras: The core problem: old methods divide by the probability that the old system showed an action. When the old system is deterministic and never shows certain actions, that probability is zero, and dividing by zero makes the estimate infinite or meaningless.

The paper's fix: don't divide by the old policy probability. Instead, reweight by the ratio of user click probabilities. If the old system showed Item 1 and the user clicked, we have evidence that Item 1 is clickable. If the new system also ranks Item 1 (or an item with similar appeal), we can estimate the new system's reward without ever asking how likely the old system was to show it.

Why this works: clicks are a measurement of user preference that exists independently of which system made the ranking. Two different deterministic systems could both show Item 1, and users would click at the same rate. But two different systems might rank Item 2 differently: one at the top (high clicks), one at the bottom (fewer clicks). The new method asks: what is the click probability of each item? How would users respond if we ranked these items in a new order? This is answerable even when the logging policy is frozen, because the answer depends on user preference, not on the old system's choices.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: old log shows Items 1, 2, 3 in that order. User clicked on Items 1 and 2, not Item 3.
Learned: Item 1 gets clicked 80% of the time, Item 2 gets clicked 70% of the time, Item 3 gets clicked 30% of the time.
New policy ranks Items 2, 1, 3 instead. Item 2 still gets clicked 70%, Item 1 still gets clicked 80%, Item 3 still 30%.
For Item 1: clicked in old log, so C_1 is 1. P_old_1 is 0.8. P_new_1 is 0.8 (same item, same appeal). Weight is 0.8 divided by 0.8 equals 1.0. Contribution is 1 times 1.0 equals 1.0.
For Item 2: clicked in old log, so C_2 is 1. P_old_2 is 0.7. P_new_2 is 0.7. Weight is 0.7 divided by 0.7 equals 1.0. Contribution is 1 times 1.0 equals 1.0.
For Item 3: not clicked in old log, so C_3 is 0. Contribution is 0 times any weight equals 0.
Sum: 1.0 plus 1.0 plus 0 equals 2.0 clicks estimated for the new policy.

math.note: The key move: each click is reweighted by how clickable that item is under the new ordering, divided by how clickable it was in the old ordering. This pivots the estimate from the system's randomness to the user's behavior.

charts.title: Old inverse propensity scoring (IPS)
charts.note: IPS assigns zero to unseen actions, creating enormous bias when logging is deterministic.

charts.title: Click-based inverse propensity scoring (CIPS)
charts.note: CIPS uses click probability, which is defined even in fully deterministic settings.

items.b: Click probabilities are estimated from data with bias.
items.html: If position bias exists (users click more on top items), the estimated click probability mixes true item appeal with position effects. The paper assumes a model can separate these, but this remains hard in practice.

items.b: New ranking must not rank unseen items.
items.html: The method works only for items the old system ranked or items similar enough to items that appear in the log. If the new policy ranks an item that never appeared in the old log, its click probability must be guessed from similar items, which adds uncertainty.

items.b: Position effects interact with click probability.
items.html: Users see items in a new order, so position bias changes. The reweighting assumes click probability is independent of position, which is not quite true. If position 1 receives more clicks than position 3 just for being first, the estimate will be off.

items.b: Method improves when click model is good.
items.html: The paper provides bounds showing bias shrinks as the click model improves, because the method's entire logic depends on knowing P(click) accurately; if the click predictor is wrong, the importance weights are wrong, so error in the model directly translates to error in the estimate. Invest in a good click predictor and the method's estimates become dependable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulated ranking environment. Create 5 items with fixed click probabilities (e.g., 0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1). Run a deterministic logging policy that always shows the same 3 items (say, items 1, 2, 3) in the same order. Log clicks. Train a click predictor model on the log to estimate each item's click probability. Now propose a new ranking (e.g., items 2, 4, 1). Use CIPS to estimate the new policy's value. Then, run the new policy on the simulator and measure actual clicks. Compare the estimate to ground truth.
demo.metric_eq: Bias of CIPS = | estimated value - true value |
demo.closing: CIPS should estimate the new policy's value within 2-5% of the true value, even when the logging policy was completely deterministic and showed only 3 out of 5 items. Old methods (IPS, ranking-wise IPS) should fail catastrophically, producing estimates off by 50%+ or infinite.
